**`CallStackMachine` (172 lines for what looks like a stack) — earned, and the problem really is this hard.** CRuby fires `:return` with `return_value = nil` for frames an exception unwound past, indistinguishable at the event from a genuine `nil`; without the per-frame raise epoch, every method that ever raised would be *asserted* to return nil — 0.4's wrong-answer-worse-than-no-answer in its purest form. And `:call` fires only after the argument prologue, so `def m(a, b = might_raise)` produces a `:return` with no `:call`, arriving in the middle of a live stack; `pop_matching`'s top-only rule is what keeps an everyday `a → b → a` chain from having every frame between the two `a`s silently deleted. The class's own comment already records that reverting `push`-for-every-call or the matching *alone* leaves the spec green because each covers the other — i.e. someone ran the unpinned-hunk sweep here and wrote down what it showed. **`@method_cache` as a two-level `ObjectSpace::WeakKeyMap` (collector.rb:47-133) — earned, and it is 軸A.** This reads like over-engineering for a memo. **Runner's four separate leak guards — earned, and each is a different leak.** `pgroup: true` + `settled` (a Ctrl-C reaching the transport thread leaves the workspace's whole test tree reparented to init, holding DB connections and ports); the bounded reap (`#run` is synchronous on the LSP transport thread, so an unbounded `waitpid` converts the timeout mechanism into "hang the editor forever"); `close!` in an `ensure` rather than after the happy path; and `discard_quietly` making each `ensure` step total so a failing first discard cannot abandon the second — or, worse, replace a propagating `Interrupt`. `unassigned_ivar_findings` (239-277) issues two independent `Prism.parse(document.text)` calls, on a document `ParserService#summarize` already parsed at engine.rb:38, to recover two facts the parser saw and discarded — which write is a write (`ivar_writes`'s own comment at 313-317 says so: "The parser records a read and a write as the same `:ivar` candidate kind ... so the writes are recovered here instead") and which names appear inside `defined?`.

Measured on `core/lib/ovallsp/server.rb` (196,586 bytes), 20 iterations each:
  Prism.parse            3.56 ms each
  ivar_writes            4.11 ms each
  ivar_names_tested      4.16 ms each
  combined per analyze   8.27 ms
One of those two parses is redundant — roughly 4.1 ms per diagnostics pass on a file that size, and it runs on every ERB view and controller the server has `assigned_ivars` for.
excess.reduction: Two, at different prices. Small: one `Prism.parse`, one visitor that collects both name sets, one `failure?` check — halves the cost and removes one of the three visitor classes, with no cross-file consequence. Structural: `ParserService` marks an `:ivar` candidate as a write and records `defined?`-tested names on the summary, and the engine reads them; that removes all three visitor classes and both parses (~50 lines) and puts the fact where the layer that sees it lives.
excess.falsifier: For the structural version: `Cache::Store#save` (store.rb:406-411) does `Marshal.dump(summary)`, so changing `ReferenceCandidate` or `FileSummary` requires bumping `Cache::Key::SCHEMA_VERSION` (currently 4) — and `CLAUDE.md` records this project being bitten by exactly that, a schema bump never made looking identical to a working cache. If the extra sets also make the cached summary materially larger, the trade may not be worth it. So the structural reduction is only correct if the schema bump lands with it and the summary-size cost is measured first. The small reduction has no such cost and is falsified only by a case where the two collectors must see different parses of the same text — there is none, and `ivar_writes` is already called first specifically so its `failure?` check gates the other.

Lines 624-626: `def simple_name_of(name); name.to_s.split("::").last.to_s; end`.

Byte-identical transformation, one written inline and one as the method that exists for it, in the same class. excess.reduction: `next unless simple_name_of(expected.name).match?(/\A[A-Z]/)`.
excess.falsifier: That the two readings must differ — e.g. if `simple_name_of` is later needed to strip only a leading `::` for the ancestor walk while the RBS-alias test still needs the last segment. Nothing in the file suggests that today, and if it becomes true the fix is to name the second rule, not to leave a silent copy.

not_excess:
Named so the next reader does not re-examine them. Each was measured, not inspected.

**`UNIVERSAL_ANCESTORS` (engine.rb:572, 575-576) — earned, but unpinned.** Prepending a `compatible_nominal?` without it left `spec/ovallsp/diagnostics` at 273/0 and `argument_type_spec.rb` at 60/0, including the Data-class and Struct-class fixtures at lines 283-284 that the comment says it exists for. Driving it showed why: `HierarchyIndex#ancestors("Point")` now returns `["::Point", "Object", "Kernel", "BasicObject"]` for `Point = Data.define(:x)`, so the stated cause was fixed upstream. It is still load-bearing for a different input — `class Orphan < Missing::Base` gives `ancestor_names("Orphan") == ["Orphan", "::Orphan", "Missing::Base", "Base"]`, and with the guard removed `Widget.new.hold(Orphan.new)` against `def hold: (Object value)` produces a false ``argument-type`` report ("`hold` expects Object here, but Orphan is given"). So: not excess. It is, by `CLAUDE.md`'s own rule, an unpinned behavioural line and therefore a defect in its own right — the fixture that was meant to distinguish the two candidate behaviours no longer can.

**The `[name] +` seed in `ancestor_names` (engine.rb:605).** Instrumented to compute the set with and without and compare on every call across 315 examples: 37 calls, one divergence, `name == "Zoo::Animal"`. Load-bearing for a nested name whose own entry's last segment is not the name.

**`NOT_A_RUBY_CLASS` applied on both the declared and the actual side (engine.rb:378, 434, 462).** Emptying the constant fails `argument_type_spec.rb:368` ("says nothing for `bool`, which converts to a name no class has"). Pinned. The apparent duplication is two different values being tested, not one rule twice.

**`receiver_type_for`'s three declines (engine.rb:761-768).** `guessed_type_name?`, `shadowed_declared_type?` and `rooted_receiver_answered_elsewhere?` all live here rather than in resolution *because* 024.47 rolled back the resolution-side placement — it broke every bare name written from inside its own namespace. Moving them is the exact reduction this project has already paid for.

**`closed_nominal?` (engine.rb:873-946).** Six of its former reasons already live at `MethodResolver#unenumerable_reason`; what remains is the Runtime Agent round trip, the ordering that makes it last (so it is asked only of receivers every cheap test already called closed), and the skip of synthesised entries. I could find nothing further to move.

**`model_resolves?`'s columns/associations arm (engine.rb:868-870).** Coverage shows line 870 never executed by 403 examples, which looks like dead code and is not. `ReferenceResolver#resolve_via_model_registry` (reference_resolver.rb:111-125) returns nil for a non-Nominal receiver, so a Union branch — `Order.recent.first.name`, 024.77's whole subject — never reaches it, and `Agent#model_method_extras` (agent.rb:427-437) returns `[[], []]` on any `StandardError` while `partial` stays false, so a model can be "closed" with an empty method list. Reachable, unpinned.

**The two uncovered `rescue` bodies (engine.rb:331 `nil`, 564 `true`).** Both are `contained` fallbacks that make the caller decline: `ivar_writes` returning nil switches the whole ivar check off, and `operator_expression?` returning true declines the argument. That is the direction §0 asks for and `rescue_verdicts.yml` requires.

**`expected_positional_types` (engine.rb:498-503).** Ruby genuinely binds trailing positionals last — `def hold(a, b = 1, c)` with two arguments binds `a` and `c` — so a fixed `required + optional` list reads the wrong parameter's type. The asymmetric handling of too-few versus too-many is likewise real: too few still binds in order, too many says nothing about which parameter the extra was for.

**`operator_expression?` parsing rather than pattern-matching (engine.rb:553-565).** The comment records the version that listed operators; the list cannot be finished. Parsing is the smaller rule.

**`declared_signature_for`'s `binding_only:` (engine.rb:1082-1120).** Two genuinely different questions over one ancestor walk, and the comment records that a third refusal (`direct`) was tried and removed for changing no answer. That is the discipline this audit is looking for, already applied.

**`SemanticContext::REQUIRED` (semantic_context.rb:26-38).** Containment at the constructor rather than a `return unless` per reader, after 0.2.9 wrote the same guard twice in `closed_nominal?`. Same shape as `Cache::Store` performing every removal in one place.

**`simple_name` (engine.rb:628-630).** Instrumenting both its call sites across 315 examples showed `delete_prefix("::")` never firing — it is a no-op for every input the suite reaches, exactly like the one `ancestor_names`'s comment already confesses to and deliberately kept. Removing defensive normalisation because no current input needs it is the 024.47-shaped move; I am not proposing it. Worth knowing, not worth changing.

**The comment density.** 11,659 of 24,172 lines are comments, and in this file nearly every one names a specific false report a specific line prevents, with the register entry. That is what made this audit possible at all, and it is not excess.
